name: Routing Table and Forwarding
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Read every field of show ip route and predict which route a router uses: longest prefix, then AD, then metric.

lesson.intro: Every routing topic on the CCNA, from static routes to OSPF, ends up as a line in the routing table, and the router uses that table to make one decision per packet. This lesson teaches you to read every field of show ip route and to predict which route wins: longest prefix match first, then administrative distance, then metric.
objectives: Identify every field in a show ip route entry: code, prefix, mask, AD, metric, next hop and exit interface
Explain where connected, local and default routes come from and what the gateway of last resort means
Predict which route a router uses for a destination with longest prefix match
Choose between competing routes to the same prefix using administrative distance and then metric

sections.title: What a router does with every packet
sections.body:
PC-A (10.1.1.10) opens a web page on a server at 10.3.3.30. The server is two routers away. PC-A compares the destination with its own subnet, sees that 10.3.3.30 is somewhere else, and sends the frame to its default gateway, R1. From there, every router repeats the same small routine until the packet arrives.

Here is that routine on R1, the way the CCNA expects you to describe it:

- **Check the frame.** R1 verifies the Ethernet FCS and silently discards a frame with errors.
- **De-encapsulate.** R1 removes the incoming Ethernet header and trailer. It only cares about the IP packet inside.
- **Choose a route.** R1 compares the destination IP address with its **routing table** and picks the best matching route. That route names a next-hop router (or says the destination is on a directly connected subnet) and an exit interface.
- **Prepare the packet.** R1 decrements the TTL. A packet whose TTL hits 0 is discarded and R1 sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message back to the source (this is exactly how traceroute discovers each hop).
- **Re-encapsulate and send.** R1 finds the MAC address of the next hop in its ARP table (sending an ARP request if it is missing), builds a brand new frame and transmits it out the exit interface.

Notice what changes and what does not. The source and destination IP addresses stay the same from PC-A to the server (unless NAT is involved). The Ethernet header is thrown away and rebuilt at every router, so the MAC addresses change on every link.

No router knows the whole path. Each one only decides the next hop, using its own routing table. That is why one wrong or missing route on one router breaks a path even when every other router is perfect, and why the rest of this lesson is about reading that table and predicting which line a router will use.
sections.code:
R1 receives a frame on G0/0 (from PC-A)
  1. FCS check passes
  2. Strip the Ethernet header and trailer
  3. Destination IP 10.3.3.30: best match in the routing table is
       O   10.3.3.0/24 [110/2] via 10.1.12.2, 00:14:22, GigabitEthernet0/1
  4. TTL 128 -> 127
  5. ARP table: 10.1.12.2 is at 5254.0012.ab02
  6. New frame out G0/1: src MAC = R1 G0/1, dst MAC = 5254.0012.ab02
     (IP header still says 10.1.1.10 -> 10.3.3.30)
sections.tip: MAC addresses change at every router hop; IP addresses stay end to end. Say it out loud until it is automatic.
sections.pitfall: Thinking a router "passes the frame along". It never forwards the incoming frame; it removes the frame, routes the packet and builds a new frame for the next link.

activity.title: Follow one packet across two routers
activity.prompt: Step through the journey. Before each step, predict which addresses change (source and destination MAC) and which stay the same (source and destination IP). Notice the two moments each router needs something: its routing table to choose the next hop, and ARP to learn that next hop's MAC.

check.question: A packet travels PC-A, R1, R2, server. Compared with the frame PC-A sent to R1, what is different in the frame R2 sends to the server?
choices: The source and destination IP addresses
Only the destination IP address
The source and destination MAC addresses
Nothing; routers forward the original frame
check.explanation: Each router builds a new frame, so both MAC addresses change on every link. The IP addresses stay the same end to end; routers read the destination IP but do not rewrite it (NAT aside).

sections.title: Reading show ip route, field by field
sections.body:
Exam questions love to paste a chunk of `show ip route` and ask what the router will do. You can only answer if every field on a line means something to you, so take this output apart once, slowly.

The **legend** at the top lists the **routing protocol codes**. You need a handful: `C` connected, `L` local, `S` static, `O` OSPF, `D` EIGRP, `B` BGP, `R` RIP, and `*` for a candidate default route. OSPF also adds qualifiers such as `IA` (inter area) and `E2` (external type 2).

The **Gateway of last resort** line tells you whether the router has a default route and where it points. More on that in its own section.

Now take one OSPF line: `O 10.1.3.0/24 [110/2] via 10.1.12.2, 00:14:22, GigabitEthernet0/1`.

- **Code** `O`: R1 learned this route from OSPF.
- **Prefix** `10.1.3.0`: the destination subnet ID. Prefix is just another name for the subnet ID.
- **Network mask** `/24`: the prefix length, shown in slash notation. It says how many leading bits of a destination must match.
- **Administrative distance** `110`: the first number in brackets. It rates how trustworthy the source of the route is.
- **Metric** `2`: the second number in brackets. The routing protocol's own cost for this path (for OSPF, the total cost).
- **Next hop** `via 10.1.12.2`: the IP address of the neighboring router to send the packet to.
- **Age** `00:14:22`: how long ago the route was learned or last changed (hours:minutes:seconds).
- **Exit interface** `GigabitEthernet0/1`: where R1 sends the packet.

The indented heading lines such as `10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 7 subnets, 3 masks` are not routes. IOS groups routes under their old classful network and tells you how many subnets and how many different masks sit inside it. "Variably subnetted" just means more than one mask is in use. When only one mask is used you see `is subnetted, 3 subnets` instead.

You can filter the table: `show ip route connected`, `show ip route static` and `show ip route ospf` show one source each, and `show ip route 10.1.3.77` tells you exactly which route the router would use for that one address.
sections.code:
R1# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is 10.1.12.2 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 10.1.12.2
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 7 subnets, 3 masks
C        10.1.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.1.3.0/24 [110/2] via 10.1.12.2, 00:14:22, GigabitEthernet0/1
O        10.1.4.0/24 [110/3] via 10.1.12.2, 00:14:22, GigabitEthernet0/1
C        10.1.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.1.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
S        10.9.9.0/24 [1/0] via 10.1.12.2
sections.tip: Read a route line left to right as a sentence: "Learned by OSPF, to reach 10.1.3.0/24, trust 110, cost 2, send to 10.1.12.2 out G0/1."
sections.pitfall: Treating the heading "10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted" as a route to 10.0.0.0/8. It is only a group label; a packet to 10.200.1.1 does not match it.

check.question: In `O 10.1.4.0/24 [110/3] via 10.1.12.2, 00:14:22, GigabitEthernet0/1`, what does the 3 tell you?
choices: The OSPF metric (total cost) of the path to 10.1.4.0/24
The administrative distance of the route
The number of routers between R1 and the subnet
The number of equal-cost paths R1 has to the subnet
check.explanation: The bracket holds [administrative distance/metric], so 110 is OSPF's AD and 3 is the OSPF cost. OSPF cost is based on bandwidth, not a count of routers, so it is not a hop count.

sections.title: Connected and local routes
sections.body:
Take a router fresh out of the box and give one interface an address. Two routes appear in the table without any routing protocol at all.

A **connected route** (code `C`) covers the whole subnet on that interface, for example `172.16.4.0/24`. It needs no next hop because the destination is right there on the link; the router can ARP for any host in it. Connected routes have an administrative distance of 0, the most trusted source there is.

A **local route** (code `L`) is a /32 host route for the router's own interface address, for example `172.16.4.1/32`. It tells the router "packets for this exact address are for me", so a ping to the router's interface is answered instead of being forwarded. IPv6 does the same thing with `L` routes of length /128.

Both appear only when two conditions hold: the interface has an IP address and it is in an up/up state. Shut the interface down or pull the cable and both routes vanish. This matters more than it looks:

- Routing protocols advertise connected subnets. If the interface is down, the subnet disappears from every other router's table too.
- A static route whose next hop sits in a connected subnet depends on that connected route existing (you will see this again in static routing).
- `show ip interface brief` is the first command to run when an expected `C` route is missing.

Connected routes are the foundation the rest of the routing table is built on. Learn to count them: one `C` and one `L` per up/up interface with an address.
sections.code:
R1(config)# interface g0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 172.16.4.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip route connected
! legend omitted
      172.16.0.0/16 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        172.16.4.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        172.16.4.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
sections.tip: Expected C route missing? Check show ip interface brief: the interface must be up/up with the address you think it has.
sections.pitfall: Expecting a connected route for an interface that is configured but down. No up/up, no C and no L route.

check.question: R1's G0/2 has 192.168.50.1/26 configured, but its cable is unplugged. What does `show ip route` list for that subnet?
choices: A C route marked inactive
Only the L route for 192.168.50.1/32
A C route with administrative distance 255
Nothing; connected and local routes exist only while the interface is up/up
check.explanation: IOS adds the C and L routes when the interface is up/up and removes both when it goes down. There is no "inactive connected route" entry, and the local route disappears together with the connected one.

sections.title: The default route and the gateway of last resort
sections.body:
A branch office has one link to headquarters. Headquarters knows 5,000 subnets. Does the branch router need 5,000 routes? No: everything that is not local goes up the same link anyway. One **default route** covers all of it.

The default route is written `0.0.0.0/0`. A /0 prefix means zero bits have to match, so it matches every destination. It is also the least specific route possible, which means the router only uses it when nothing more specific matches (the next section makes that precise).

The line **Gateway of last resort** reports the default route the router is currently using:

- `Gateway of last resort is 10.0.0.1 to network 0.0.0.0` means a default route exists and points to next hop 10.0.0.1.
- `Gateway of last resort is not set` means there is no default route. A packet that matches no route is discarded, and the router normally sends an ICMP Destination Unreachable message back to the source.

The default route itself carries an asterisk, the "candidate default" mark. Where it came from shows in the code:

- `S*` a static default you configured with `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop>` (AD 1).
- `O*E2` a default advertised into OSPF by another router with `default-information originate`.
- `S*` with `[254/0]` a default learned from DHCP on an interface that gets its address from an ISP.

One router's default route says nothing about the hosts behind it: PCs have their own default gateway setting. The gateway of last resort is the router's own "if all else fails, send it here".
sections.code:
Branch# show ip route
! legend omitted
Gateway of last resort is 10.0.0.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 10.0.0.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 4 subnets, 3 masks
C        10.0.0.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.0.0.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        10.5.5.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.5.5.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1

Core# show ip route | include Gateway
Gateway of last resort is not set
sections.tip: 0.0.0.0/0 matches everything and loses to everything. It is a safety net, not a preference.
sections.pitfall: Reading "Gateway of last resort is not set" as a problem with the hosts. It is the router's own default route that is missing, so unknown destinations are dropped at this router.

check.question: Core shows `Gateway of last resort is not set`. A packet arrives for 8.8.8.8 and no route matches it. What does Core do?
choices: Floods the packet out every interface except the one it arrived on
Discards the packet and normally sends ICMP Destination Unreachable to the source
Forwards it to the neighbor with the highest router ID
Forwards it out the interface with the most bandwidth
check.explanation: With no matching route and no default route there is nowhere to send the packet, so the router drops it and reports the failure with ICMP. Flooding is switch behavior for unknown MAC addresses, not router behavior for unknown IP destinations.

sections.title: Rule 1: longest prefix match
sections.body:
R1's table below has five routes that all overlap. A packet arrives for 172.16.1.1. Which route does R1 use?

Start by writing down the range of addresses each route matches:

- `172.16.1.1/32` matches only 172.16.1.1 (a host route).
- `172.16.1.0/24` matches 172.16.1.0 to 172.16.1.255.
- `172.16.0.0/22` matches 172.16.0.0 to 172.16.3.255.
- `172.16.0.0/16` matches 172.16.0.0 to 172.16.255.255.
- `0.0.0.0/0` matches every address.

172.16.1.1 falls inside all five ranges. The rule is simple: **when several routes match, the router uses the most specific one, the route with the longest prefix length.** So 172.16.1.1 uses the /32. A few more:

- 172.16.1.200 matches the /24, /22, /16 and /0. The /24 wins.
- 172.16.3.9 matches the /22, /16 and /0 (it is outside 172.16.1.0/24). The /22 wins.
- 172.16.4.1 is outside the /22 (which ends at 172.16.3.255), so the /16 wins.
- 192.168.9.9 matches only the default route.

Look at what did not matter: the code letter, the AD and the metric. The /32 is a static route with AD 1 and the /24 is OSPF with AD 110, but that is irrelevant because they are different prefixes. Longest prefix match always comes first. A static /16 never beats an OSPF /24 for an address inside that /24.

The method on the exam: find every route whose range contains the destination (subnetting math), then pick the largest number after the slash. If you are on a real router, `show ip route 172.16.3.9` does the work for you and prints the route that wins.
sections.code:
R1# show ip route
! legend omitted, connected routes omitted
Gateway of last resort is 10.0.0.2 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 10.0.0.2
      172.16.0.0/16 is variably subnetted, 4 subnets, 4 masks
O        172.16.0.0/16 [110/4] via 10.0.0.6, 00:03:11, GigabitEthernet0/2
O        172.16.0.0/22 [110/3] via 10.0.0.10, 00:03:11, GigabitEthernet0/3
O        172.16.1.0/24 [110/2] via 10.0.0.14, 00:03:11, GigabitEthernet0/4
S        172.16.1.1/32 [1/0] via 10.0.0.18
sections.tip: Convert each route to an address range first. Once the ranges are written down, the longest prefix that contains the destination jumps out.
sections.pitfall: Choosing the route with the lowest AD or lowest metric when the prefixes have different lengths. A more specific prefix wins before AD or metric are ever looked at.

activity.title: Pick the winning route
activity.prompt: For each destination, first list every route whose range contains the address, then pick the longest prefix. Only reach for administrative distance or metric when two candidates have exactly the same prefix and length. Try to finish five destinations without a wrong pick.

check.question: Using R1's table above, which route does R1 use for a packet to 172.16.3.9?
check.explanation: 172.16.0.0/22 covers 172.16.0.0 to 172.16.3.255, so it contains 172.16.3.9, and it is longer than the /16 and the /0 that also match. The /24 covers only 172.16.1.x, so it does not match at all.

sections.title: Rule 2: administrative distance
sections.body:
R1 runs OSPF and EIGRP (maybe during a migration), and someone also typed a static route. All three know a way to 10.50.0.0/16: the exact same prefix and length. A routing table can hold only one source's route for a given prefix, so which one goes in?

Metrics cannot settle it. OSPF's cost of 20 and EIGRP's metric of 3,072 are calculated from different formulas, so comparing them is meaningless. Instead IOS uses **administrative distance (AD)**: a number that rates how believable each source of routing information is. **Lower is better.** The static route (AD 1) beats EIGRP (AD 90), which beats OSPF (AD 110).

The defaults below are worth memorizing; the exam quotes them freely.

Three details that trip people up:

- AD only compares routes for the **exact same prefix and prefix length**. A static 10.0.0.0/8 (AD 1) and an OSPF 10.1.1.0/24 (AD 110) are different routes and both get installed. For 10.1.1.5, longest prefix match then picks the OSPF /24.
- AD is local to one router. It is never advertised to neighbors. Changing AD on R1 changes only R1's choices.
- The losing routes are not forgotten. They stay in the protocol's own database (the OSPF LSDB, the EIGRP topology table), ready to be installed if the winner disappears. That is the whole trick behind floating static routes: a static route given a higher AD than OSPF sits out until the OSPF route vanishes.

AD 255 means "do not believe this at all": a route with AD 255 is never installed.
sections.code:
Route source                    Default AD
Connected interface                 0
Static route                        1
eBGP (external BGP)                20
EIGRP (internal)                   90
OSPF                              110
IS-IS                             115
RIP                               120
EIGRP (external)                  170
iBGP (internal BGP)               200
DHCP-learned default route        254
Unknown / unusable                255   (never installed)
sections.tip: Memory hook: 0 connected, 1 static, 20 eBGP, 90 EIGRP, 110 OSPF, 120 RIP, 200 iBGP, 255 never.
sections.pitfall: Applying AD to routes with different prefix lengths. AD only breaks ties between sources offering the exact same prefix/length; otherwise longest prefix match decides.

check.question: R1 learns 10.50.0.0/16 from OSPF and from EIGRP, and also has a static route for 10.50.0.0/16, all with default settings. Which one is installed?
choices: The EIGRP route, because AD 90 is the lowest dynamic AD
The OSPF route, because OSPF has the best metric
All three, so the router can load balance
The static route, because AD 1 is the lowest
check.explanation: Same prefix and length from three sources, so AD decides and lower wins: static 1, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110. Routers never load balance across different routing sources, and metrics from different protocols are never compared.

sections.title: Rule 3: metric, equal-cost paths and the full decision
sections.body:
Now one protocol knows two ways to the same prefix. OSPF on R1 calculates a path to 10.4.4.0/24 through R2 with cost 3 and another through R3 with cost 5. OSPF offers the routing table only its best path: the lowest **metric** wins, so the cost 3 route through R2 is installed.

Each protocol measures "best" its own way:

- OSPF: cost, the sum of interface costs along the path, based on bandwidth.
- EIGRP: a composite metric, by default from the slowest bandwidth and total delay of the path.
- RIP: hop count, the number of routers to cross.

When two paths from the same protocol tie on metric, the router installs both and load balances across them. This is **equal-cost multipath (ECMP)**; OSPF installs up to four equal-cost paths by default (the `maximum-paths` setting). In `show ip route` the route appears once with two "via" lines.

Putting the three rules together, the way the CCNA blueprint words it:

- **Longest prefix match** first: among all routes that contain the destination, the most specific wins.
- **Administrative distance** next: when different sources offer the same prefix and length, the lowest AD source is the one in the table.
- **Metric** last: within one protocol, the lowest metric path is installed, and equal metrics share the load.

Under the hood, AD and metric are applied when the router builds its table (they decide which route for each prefix gets in), and longest prefix match is applied to every packet against the routes that made it in. Thinking of it that way makes tricky questions easy: first ask "which routes are actually in the table?", then ask "which of those is the longest match for this packet?".
sections.code:
R1# show ip route ospf
! legend omitted, other routes omitted
O        10.4.4.0/24 [110/3] via 10.1.13.3, 00:01:12, GigabitEthernet0/2
                     [110/3] via 10.1.12.2, 00:01:12, GigabitEthernet0/1

R1# show ip route 10.4.4.0
Routing entry for 10.4.4.0/24
  Known via "ospf 1", distance 110, metric 3, type intra area
  Last update from 10.1.13.3 on GigabitEthernet0/2, 00:01:12 ago
  Routing Descriptor Blocks:
  * 10.1.13.3, from 3.3.3.3, 00:01:12 ago, via GigabitEthernet0/2
      Route metric is 3, traffic share count is 1
    10.1.12.2, from 2.2.2.2, 00:01:12 ago, via GigabitEthernet0/1
      Route metric is 3, traffic share count is 1
sections.tip: AD compares between sources; metric compares within one protocol. If two routes come from different protocols, their metrics never meet.
sections.pitfall: Comparing an OSPF cost with an EIGRP metric or a RIP hop count. Different protocols, different scales: that is exactly why AD exists.

check.question: OSPF on R1 finds three paths to 10.4.4.0/24 with costs 3, 3 and 5. What ends up in the routing table?
choices: Both cost-3 paths, used together for load balancing
Only the first cost-3 path that OSPF calculated
All three paths, with traffic weighted by cost
Only the cost-5 path, because a higher metric is better
check.explanation: OSPF installs the lowest-cost path, and when several paths tie at the lowest cost it installs all of them (up to maximum-paths, 4 by default) and load balances. The cost-5 path loses, and OSPF does not do unequal-cost load balancing.

keyTerms.definition: The list of routes a router uses to choose the next hop and exit interface for each packet.
The subnet ID part of a route, such as 10.1.3.0 in 10.1.3.0/24.
The number after the slash: how many leading bits of the destination must match the route.
The IP address of the neighboring router a packet is sent to, shown as "via" in show ip route.
Code C: the subnet of an up/up interface with an IP address, AD 0.
Code L: a /32 (IPv6 /128) host route for the router's own interface address.
The default route (0.0.0.0/0) the router currently uses for destinations nothing else matches.
When several routes contain the destination, the router uses the one with the longest prefix length.
A local trust rating for each route source; lower wins when sources offer the same prefix.
A routing protocol's cost for a path, compared only between paths from the same protocol.
Equal-cost multipath: several paths with the same best metric installed together for load balancing.

summary: Routers strip the incoming frame, route the packet on its destination IP and build a new frame, so MACs change per hop and IPs do not.
A route line reads: code, prefix/length, [AD/metric], via next hop, age, exit interface.
Each addressed up/up interface adds a C route for its subnet and an L /32 route for its own address.
0.0.0.0/0 matches everything and loses to everything; "Gateway of last resort is not set" means unmatched packets are dropped.
Longest prefix match always comes first; AD only compares sources for the identical prefix, and metric only compares paths within one protocol.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how a router decides where to send a packet to 172.16.1.9 when its table holds a default route, a static 172.16.0.0/16 and an OSPF 172.16.1.0/24, and why administrative distance and metric never get a say in that particular choice.

questions.question: A router forwards a packet from one Ethernet LAN to another. What does it do with the incoming frame's Ethernet header?
choices: Keeps it and only updates the destination MAC address
Keeps it unchanged so the receiver can see the original sender
Discards it and builds a new frame for the outgoing link
Converts it into the IP header of the outgoing packet
questions.explanation: Routers de-encapsulate: the incoming data-link header and trailer are removed, the packet is routed, and a new frame is built for the next link. That is why MAC addresses change at every hop while IP addresses do not.

questions.question: Put R1's steps for forwarding one received frame in order.
items: Check the FCS and discard the frame if it has errors
Remove the incoming Ethernet header and trailer
Match the destination IP address against the routing table
Find the next hop's MAC address in the ARP table (or ARP for it)
Build a new frame and transmit it out the exit interface
questions.explanation: Error check first, then de-encapsulate, then route on the destination IP, then resolve the next hop's MAC and re-encapsulate. ARP comes after the routing decision because the router needs the route to know which next hop to ARP for.

questions.question: PC-A (10.1.1.10/24, gateway 10.1.1.1) sends a packet to 10.3.3.30, two routers away. Which destination MAC address does PC-A put in the frame?
choices: The MAC address of the server 10.3.3.30
The broadcast address FFFF.FFFF.FFFF
The MAC address of the last router before the server
The MAC address of its default gateway, 10.1.1.1
questions.explanation: The destination is off-subnet, so PC-A sends the frame to its default gateway: destination IP 10.3.3.30, destination MAC of 10.1.1.1. PC-A cannot ARP for a host in another subnet, and it has no idea which router is last on the path.

questions.question: A packet arrives at R2 with a TTL of 1 and a destination two hops further on. What does R2 do?
choices: Forwards it with a TTL of 0 so the next router can drop it
Discards it and sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message to the source
Resets the TTL to 255 and forwards it
Discards it silently without telling anyone
questions.explanation: Decrementing 1 gives 0, so R2 must drop the packet. It reports this with ICMP Time Exceeded, which is how traceroute learns the address of each hop. A packet is never forwarded with TTL 0.

questions.question: Match each routing table code to its meaning.

pairs.right: Subnet on one of the router's own up/up interfaces
The router's own interface address as a host route
Configured with the ip route command

questions.explanation: These codes start every line of show ip route. C and L appear automatically for addressed up/up interfaces, S comes from configuration, O and D from routing protocols, and the asterisk marks a route that can serve as the default.

questions.question: Which statement about this route is true?
questions.code:
R1# show ip route ospf
! legend omitted
O        10.1.4.0/24 [110/3] via 10.1.12.2, 00:14:22, GigabitEthernet0/1
choices: The route has administrative distance 3 and metric 110
10.1.12.2 is R1's own address on G0/1
R1 sends packets for 10.1.4.0/24 to 10.1.12.2 out G0/1, and OSPF rates the path at cost 3
The route expires in 14 minutes and 22 seconds
questions.explanation: The bracket is [AD/metric], so AD is 110 and the cost is 3. "via 10.1.12.2" is the neighbor's address (the next hop), and 00:14:22 is how long ago the route was learned, not a countdown.

questions.question: Using the output, what is the administrative distance of the route R1 uses for 10.9.9.0/24?
questions.code:
R1# show ip route static
! legend omitted
S        10.9.9.0/24 [1/0] via 10.1.12.2
questions.explanation: The first number in brackets is the AD. The S code marks a static route, and static routes default to AD 1; the metric of a static route is 0.

questions.question: Which three pieces of information appear on an OSPF route line in show ip route? Choose three.
choices: The next-hop IP address
The router ID of the router that advertised the route
The exit interface
The next hop's MAC address
The administrative distance
questions.explanation: An OSPF line shows code, prefix/length, [AD/metric], via next-hop IP, age and exit interface. The advertising router's ID appears in show ip route <prefix> detail and in the LSDB, and MAC addresses live in the ARP table, not the routing table.

questions.question: Type the command that lists only the OSPF-learned routes in R1's IPv4 routing table.
questions.explanation: show ip route accepts a source keyword such as connected, static or ospf to filter the output. Abbreviations like sh ip ro ospf also work.

questions.question: A packet arrives for 172.16.200.1. Based only on this output, which statement is true?
questions.code:
R1# show ip route
! legend omitted
Gateway of last resort is not set

      172.16.0.0/16 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        172.16.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        172.16.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
choices: No route matches, because the heading line is not a route and none of the listed subnets contains 172.16.200.1
It matches 172.16.0.0/16, the heading line
It matches 172.16.1.0/24 because that is the closest subnet
It matches both subnets and is load balanced
questions.explanation: The indented "172.16.0.0/16 is variably subnetted" line is a group label for the classful network, not a route. 172.16.200.1 is outside 172.16.1.0/24 and 172.16.1.1/32, and there is no default route, so the packet is dropped. Routers never pick the "closest" subnet; a route either contains the address or it does not.

questions.question: What is a local route, code L, in show ip route?
choices: A route to a subnet on a neighboring router
A static route that points out a local interface
A /32 host route for one of the router's own interface addresses
A route used only for management traffic
questions.explanation: Local routes match exactly the router's own IP address on an interface (/32 in IPv4, /128 in IPv6) so the router knows to process those packets itself. The connected route (C) covers the rest of that subnet.

questions.question: R1 has `C 10.1.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1`. An engineer shuts down G0/1. What happens to that route and to R1's `L 10.1.12.1/32` route?
choices: The C route is removed but the L route stays
Both are removed from the routing table
Both stay but are marked down
Both stay until the ARP entries time out
questions.explanation: Connected and local routes exist only while the interface is up/up. Shutting it down removes both immediately, and any routing protocol advertising that subnet withdraws it too.

questions.question: Based on this output, how many connected (C) routes does R1 have?
questions.code:
R1# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     10.1.1.1        YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     10.1.12.1       YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     10.1.99.1       YES manual administratively down down
Loopback0              1.1.1.1         YES manual up                    up
questions.explanation: Only addressed interfaces in an up/up state create connected routes: G0/0, G0/1 and Loopback0. G0/2 is administratively down, so its subnet is not in the table.

questions.question: Why does IOS add a local /32 route for each interface address?
choices: So the router can advertise its address into OSPF
So hosts can use the address as a default gateway
So the router can ARP for its own address
So packets addressed to the router itself match a route that says "deliver to me" instead of being forwarded
questions.explanation: A packet to 172.16.4.1 would otherwise match the connected /24 and look like it should be sent onto the LAN. The /32 local route is longer, wins by longest prefix match, and tells IOS to process the packet locally.

questions.question: In show ipv6 route, what prefix length does the local (L) route for the router's own interface address use?
questions.explanation: IPv6 local routes are host routes for the router's own address, so they use /128, the IPv6 equivalent of the IPv4 /32.

questions.question: Which destination addresses does the route 0.0.0.0/0 match?
choices: Only the address 0.0.0.0
Only addresses on directly connected subnets
Every IPv4 address, but it is used only when no more specific route matches
Only public internet addresses
questions.explanation: A /0 prefix means zero bits must match, so every address matches. Because it is the shortest possible prefix, longest prefix match picks it only as a last resort.

questions.question: R1 receives a packet for 10.3.3.3. What does it do?
questions.code:
R1# show ip route
! legend omitted
Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 3 subnets, 3 masks
C        10.1.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.2.0.0/16 [110/2] via 10.1.12.2, 00:20:10, GigabitEthernet0/1
O     172.16.0.0/16 [110/3] via 10.1.12.2, 00:20:10, GigabitEthernet0/1
choices: Discards it, because no route contains 10.3.3.3 and there is no default route
Forwards it via 10.1.12.2 using 10.2.0.0/16, the nearest subnet
Forwards it out G0/0, the connected 10.x subnet
Floods it out all interfaces
questions.explanation: 10.3.3.3 is not in 10.1.1.0/24, 10.2.0.0/16 (10.2.0.0 to 10.2.255.255) or 172.16.0.0/16, and the gateway of last resort is not set. Having routes for other 10.x subnets does not help; the address must fall inside a route's range.

questions.question: In `S* 0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 10.0.0.1`, what does the asterisk mean?
choices: The route is the best of several equal-cost paths
The route was configured with the permanent keyword
The route is currently down and will be removed
The route is a candidate default route
questions.explanation: The legend lists * as "candidate default". The Gateway of last resort line then shows which candidate is actually in use.

questions.question: Branch router B1 shows this route. How did B1 most likely get it?
questions.code:
B1# show ip route ospf
! legend omitted
Gateway of last resort is 10.1.12.1 to network 0.0.0.0

O*E2  0.0.0.0/0 [110/1] via 10.1.12.1, 00:20:51, GigabitEthernet0/1/0
choices: B1 has a static default route configured toward 10.1.12.1
Another OSPF router with its own default route advertised it with default-information originate
B1 learned the default from a DHCP server on G0/1/0
It is an intra-area OSPF route for the 0.0.0.0 subnet
questions.explanation: O means OSPF, * means candidate default, and E2 means OSPF external type 2, which is how default-information originate advertises 0.0.0.0/0 (metric 1 by default). A static default would show S*, and a DHCP-learned default shows S* with AD 254.

questions.question: R1 has routes for 10.0.0.0/8, 10.1.0.0/16, 10.1.1.0/24 and 0.0.0.0/0. Which route does it use for 10.1.1.10?
questions.explanation: All four routes contain 10.1.1.10, and the router uses the one with the longest prefix, /24. The others are less specific and lose regardless of their AD or metric.

questions.question: Using this table, which next hop does R1 use for a packet to 172.16.1.200?
questions.explanation: 172.16.1.200 is in 172.16.1.0/24, 172.16.0.0/22, 172.16.0.0/16 and the default. The /24 is longest, so the next hop is 10.0.0.14. The /32 matches only 172.16.1.1, not .200.

questions.question: Using the same table, which next hop does R1 use for a packet to 172.16.4.1?
questions.explanation: 172.16.0.0/22 covers 172.16.0.0 to 172.16.3.255, so 172.16.4.1 is just outside it. The longest remaining match is 172.16.0.0/16 via 10.0.0.6. The default route would only be used if the /16 were missing.

questions.question: R2 has these routes. Which next hop does it use for 192.168.23.5?
questions.explanation: /22 blocks step by 4 in the third octet, so 192.168.20.0/22 covers 192.168.20.0 to 192.168.23.255 and contains .23.5. The /20 (16.0 to 31.255) and /16 also match but are shorter. 192.168.24.0/21 starts at .24.0, so it does not match.

questions.question: A packet is addressed to 10.20.30.40. Which of these routes contain that address? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 10.20.30.64/26 covers .64 to .127, so .40 is outside it, and 10.20.31.0/24 is a different third octet. The /8, /16, /24 and the default all contain the address; the router would use the /24.

questions.question: R1 has `S 10.0.0.0/8 [1/0] via 10.9.9.1` and `O 10.1.1.0/24 [110/20] via 10.8.8.1`. Which next hop does R1 use for 10.1.1.5?
choices: 10.9.9.1, because the static route has the lower AD
10.8.8.1, because the OSPF /24 is the longer match
10.9.9.1, because the static route has the lower metric
Both, load balanced, because both routes match
questions.explanation: These are different prefixes, so both routes are in the table and AD never comes into play. Longest prefix match picks the /24. AD would only matter if both sources offered 10.1.1.0/24 exactly.

questions.question: Match each route source to its default administrative distance.
questions.explanation: Lower AD means more believable. These six values come up constantly on the exam; also remember iBGP 200 and 255 for a source that is never trusted.

questions.question: What is the default administrative distance of a route learned from internal BGP (iBGP)?
questions.explanation: eBGP routes get AD 20 and iBGP routes get 200. The large gap makes routes learned from an IGP like OSPF (110) preferred over iBGP routes for the same prefix.

questions.question: R1 learns 10.5.0.0/16 from EIGRP with metric 3,072 and from OSPF with cost 2. Both use default AD. Which route is installed?
choices: The OSPF route, because a cost of 2 is lower than 3,072
Both routes, load balanced
The EIGRP route, because its AD of 90 is lower than OSPF's 110
The OSPF route, because OSPF is an open standard
questions.explanation: When different protocols offer the same prefix and length, AD decides. Metrics from different protocols are calculated differently and are never compared, so the small OSPF cost means nothing here.

questions.question: An engineer changes the administrative distance of OSPF on R1 to 95. What effect does this have on R2, R1's OSPF neighbor?
choices: None; AD is a local setting used only by R1 when it chooses between sources
R2 also starts using 95 for OSPF routes learned from R1
R2 rejects R1's routes because the AD values no longer match
R2 prefers routes learned from R1 over other OSPF neighbors
questions.explanation: Administrative distance is never carried in routing updates. Each router applies its own AD values when deciding which source to believe. AD is not one of the settings that must match between OSPF neighbors.

questions.question: Why can't a router simply compare metrics to choose between an OSPF route and an EIGRP route to the same prefix?
questions.answer: Each protocol calculates its metric with a different formula (OSPF from interface costs, EIGRP from bandwidth and delay), so the numbers are on different scales. Administrative distance is the tie breaker between sources; metric only compares paths within one protocol.
questions.explanation: This is the core reason the decision has separate AD and metric steps. AD compares sources, metric compares paths inside one source.

questions.question: What does this output tell you about how R1 forwards traffic to 10.4.4.0/24?
questions.code:
R1# show ip route ospf
! legend omitted
O        10.4.4.0/24 [110/3] via 10.1.13.3, 00:01:12, GigabitEthernet0/2
                     [110/3] via 10.1.12.2, 00:01:12, GigabitEthernet0/1
choices: R1 load balances across two equal-cost OSPF paths, via 10.1.13.3 and via 10.1.12.2
R1 uses 10.1.13.3 and keeps 10.1.12.2 as a standby path
R1 has two different routes, one static and one OSPF
The second line is a stale route that will be removed
questions.explanation: One route with two "via" lines and identical [110/3] values is equal-cost multipath. OSPF installs up to four equal-cost paths by default and the router shares traffic across them.

questions.question: Put the tie breakers in the order the CCNA blueprint uses for choosing a route.
items: Load balance across paths that still tie
questions.explanation: Longest prefix first, then AD to pick between sources for the same prefix, then metric within one protocol. If metrics still tie, the protocol installs the equal-cost paths and the router load balances.

questions.question: R1's table is shown. A packet for 10.8.8.8 is routed via 10.0.0.6. Then the OSPF neighbor 10.0.0.6 fails and its route is withdrawn. Which next hop does R1 use for the next packet to 10.8.8.8?
questions.code:
R1# show ip route
! legend omitted, connected routes omitted
Gateway of last resort is 10.0.0.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 10.0.0.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 8 subnets, 4 masks
S        10.8.0.0/16 [1/0] via 10.0.0.2
O        10.8.8.0/24 [110/20] via 10.0.0.6, 00:05:01, GigabitEthernet0/2
choices: 10.0.0.1, using the default route
None; the packet is dropped until OSPF reconverges
10.0.0.2, using the static 10.8.0.0/16 route
10.0.0.6, because static routes do not change
questions.explanation: While the OSPF /24 exists it wins by longest prefix. Once it is withdrawn, the longest remaining match for 10.8.8.8 is the static /16, which is still more specific than the default route.

questions.question: Type the command that shows exactly which route R1 uses to reach the address 10.4.4.20.
questions.explanation: Giving show ip route a single address makes IOS do the longest prefix match for you and print the matching entry, including its source, AD, metric and next hops.
